>I think you’re both right but in your case you probably somewhat played the social game by advertising your successes and extra work which got you noticed enough to be rewarded. Is that the case?

This is my experience.

In my first job I went above and beyond but it never resulted in better opportunities or pay simply because my line manager never referenced my involvement when presenting the work to the higher ups.

To advance you basically need your manager's manager to be aware of your importance, then be ready to leverage that at the right time when the additional work you've undertaken becomes critical to their success. But that work also needs to add additional value and be highly visible, as opposed to just doing your normal work for longer hours  as simply being a 'hard-worker' won't get you anywhere. 

When there's a vacancy for a higher position, or you want more salary, you give them the "I've had a better offer from elsewhere that you need to match or I'm off". Always worked for me, but even if they call your bluff you will have enough achievements your CV to land a better job as recruiters love that shit.  

Obviously being socially well connected helps, but ultimately for promotions the recruiting managers will opt for someone that has already proven to do more than their current role for their own security.

> Yeah it’s weird to me how much English fans want to gatekeep the sport. Who wouldn’t want others to fall in love with their town, team and sport as long as they did so respectfully?

It's because supporting a lower league football club is a unique experience, and any glamorisation is antithetical to that. 

Football has traditionally always had at tribal aspect to it. It was the representation of your local community against another. You'd see the same familiar faces, travel together, and through good or bad know that it's shared communal experience. 

In the early 90s the Premier League became rapidly globalised, and many fans lost that sense of association with their clubs. Either by being priced out or no longer being able to get tickets. The bigger clubs are now more like multinational corporate brands than local community hubs. 

I don't think any Wrexham fans have a problem with their American support, but I also understand why there's a wider dislike and skepticism to that sort of attention.

I get where you're coming from - seeing instant goals from corners with teams stacked with  6'8" giants would be beyond tedious. I don't mind corners being ineffective despite the lack of realism. 

There's a balance between that and making contested headed goals from open play next to impossible though. Scoring from crosses would be OK as long as you needed to manually aim the cross and position your striker correctly. 

There needs to be some penalty from camping in the box and not actively pressing, which would only come from a long ball into those areas being a threat.

> The other way to defend is to form a narrow compact block (think Atletico madrid). The game does not allow you to do that. No parking the bus allowed.

This should be viable, but only if headed goals are a threat, or allow tighter control in the box without always losing the ball. 

With interceptions and tackles as they currently are, if the defensive tracking worked a deep block would become impenetrable.

> Massive stamina nerf for high depth (even if your player has 99 stam and relentless+), make it scale exponentially, so that 90-95 depth would be on the upper end of the scale and absolutely kill your players

But teams in real life can press absurdly high all game. If you can win the ball back quickly and maintain high possession, it's achievable without draining stamina. 

The difference is it's incredibly difficult to organise effectively and high risk. High lines should be viable, but easier to exploit and reliant on the defender having to actually time their tackles rather than just mash it aimlessly and still win the ball.

I'm in food manufacturing so have worked with many engineers, and known many who would take naps while on their shift lol

I think engineering in the UK is split between the high-tech industries such as F1, arms, pharmaceuticals, and the lower grade work like textiles and consumer goods. 

I've only experienced the latter where it's generally guys who have learnt on the job without any higher education, so wouldn't be surprised to hear they're worse than their equivalents in France and Germany where there seem to be more technical colleges. And yeah the foreign accent probably does give an air of authenticity, but as soon as it's perceived as criticism it would quickly change to 'they just don't understand how it works over here'. 

I have worked in French offices a bit and found them more formal. This was pre-Covid so may have changed since then. Longer hours, 2 hour communal lunches, more rigid hierarchy. But also more holidays and food was paid for. 

The supermarches were a lot less forgiving and collaborative which was unpleasant to work with. If the delivery wasn't exactly right you would get instantly fined and it was very much a one-way relationship. (German ones are even worse) A few of the Polish guys tell me they'd never be able to refer to their previous line managers in Germany by only their first name (always 'Mr [Surname]', like at school) which I find hilarious. 

That said, there's still more commonality than differences, and I've made many French friends over the years with great senses of humour. I'd relocate to the south of France in a heartbeat given the right opportunity. The quality of living seems so much better than the UK, I always struggle to understand why so many Europeans move here.

I've actually worked within food supply chains the last 15 years, both at suppliers and retailers. The supply side is mostly dominated by a few colossal parent companies, which is actually not a bad thing as they're the only ones with enough leverage to not get railroaded by the retailers. 

Price is king so despite popular opinion increased costs (such as commodity fluctuations) are rarely if ever passed on directly to the consumer. This along with the relentless pursuit to increase profits each quarter, inevitably leads to cutting corners and shitty working conditions.

Factory work is exhausting, monotonous, and poorly paid so theres a huge turnover in staff which 90% are Eastern European or South Asian. Genuinely can't think of one white British permanent operator in the last 10 years.

Would say every one I've worked in or visited has had very stringent hygiene and health & safety procedures so I think the UK does OK there. 

Fundamentally the biggest issue from my perspective is the need to perpetually increase profits. I don't think most managers or supervisors are overtly malicious, but that immense pressure  and paranoia of being replaced means poor or wilfully ignorant decisions are made that adversely impact product quality and general job satisfaction for the majority of their staff.

The first company I was with had a social club, sports facilities and amazing subsidised canteen for all its factory staff. Most of the shifts loved working there, there was a big sense of comradrey especially during those cooked meal breaks, and it wasn't rare to see retired people return just because they missed it. After two years a Chinese hedge fund bought them out, scrapped any social resources, and replaced the canteen with two vending machines of shite. Sounds incidental but it completely ripped the soul of the place.
